promptText: What is the fundamental difference between props and state in a React component?
options: Props are read-only values passed down from a parent; state is data the component owns and manages internally, updated via a setter
Props can be changed by the component itself; state can only be changed by the parent
State is always derived from props automatically
Props and state are two names for the exact same mechanism
explanation: Props flow down from the parent and are immutable from the receiving component's perspective; state is local data the component owns and updates itself, and changing it (via useState's setter, for instance) triggers a re-render.

promptText: Why does React require a `key` prop when rendering a list of elements?
options: Keys are purely cosmetic and only affect developer tooling, not behavior
Keys give each list item a stable identity so React's reconciler can tell which items were added, removed, or reordered, instead of re-rendering the whole list from scratch
Keys are required only for lists longer than 10 items
Keys determine the visual order in which items are painted on screen
explanation: During reconciliation, React matches old and new children by key to determine what actually changed; without stable keys, React falls back to matching by position, which can misattribute DOM nodes and internal state to the wrong logical item.

promptText: What distinguishes a controlled input from an uncontrolled input in React?
options: A controlled input's value lives in React state (driven by `value` + `onChange`); an uncontrolled input keeps its value in the DOM itself, read via a ref when needed
Controlled inputs cannot have an onChange handler
Uncontrolled inputs automatically validate themselves
Controlled inputs only work with text fields, never checkboxes or selects
explanation: A controlled input makes React the single source of truth for its value via the value prop and an onChange handler; an uncontrolled input lets the DOM manage its own value, which you read on demand through a ref (using defaultValue for the initial value).

promptText: Why would you use `<>...</>` (a Fragment) instead of wrapping sibling elements in a `<div>`?
options: Fragments render faster than any other DOM element in all cases

Fragments let you group multiple children without adding any extra node to the DOM, avoiding wrapper divs that can break CSS layouts (flexbox/grid) or invalid HTML nesting (like wrapping `<td>` elements)
Fragments automatically add a unique key to every child
Fragments are required any time a component returns more than one line of JSX
explanation: A component must return a single root, but Fragments provide that grouping with zero DOM footprint, avoiding wrapper divs that can break layouts depending on direct parent-child CSS relationships or produce invalid HTML nesting.

promptText: Why does incrementing `countRef.current++` inside an event handler fail to update what's displayed on screen, unlike calling a state setter?
options: Refs can only hold string values, not numbers

Mutating a ref's .current property is intentionally invisible to React's render cycle — it never schedules a re-render, unlike a state setter, which is why refs are for values the render doesn't need to reflect, not for UI-visible data
countRef.current++ is a syntax error in React components
Refs are reset to their initial value on every render
explanation: useRef gives you a mutable container whose changes are deliberately invisible to React — writing .current never triggers a re-render. Anything the UI should visibly reflect needs to be state (useState), not a ref.

promptText: How does a child component in React communicate a change back up to its parent, given that data only flows down via props?
options: The child directly mutates a prop object it received
The parent passes a callback function down as a prop; the child calls that function (often with some data) to request a change, and the parent updates its own state in response
React automatically synchronizes any local child state back into the parent's state
The child dispatches a native DOM event that the parent's render function listens for
explanation: Since props only flow downward, the accepted pattern is for the parent to hand the child a callback prop (e.g. onSelect); the child invokes that function to notify the parent, and the parent decides how to update its own state — keeping data flow strictly one-directional.

promptText: A list of text inputs is keyed by array index: `items.map((item, i) => <input key={i} defaultValue={item.name} />)`. What concrete bug occurs when a new item is prepended to the top of the array?
options: Nothing breaks; index keys work correctly for any insertion position

Because React matches elements by key/position, prepending shifts every item's index, so React reuses each existing DOM node (and its in-progress typed value) at the new index — the typed text visually 'sticks' to the wrong logical item instead of following its original data
React throws a runtime error immediately when an index key changes
The entire list unmounts and remounts on every keystroke
explanation: With index keys, prepending an item shifts every other item's index, and React interprets 'same key at this position' as 'same logical item' — so the DOM node (and any in-progress input value) that used to represent item 0 now gets reused for the newly-different item at index 0, producing the classic misattributed-state bug.

promptText: Why does `setTodos(todos)` after `todos.push(newItem)` fail to reliably trigger a re-render, even though the array's contents visibly changed?
options: push() returns a boolean instead of the array, so setTodos receives the wrong type

React compares the new state to the old state by reference using Object.is; since push() mutates the array in place, the reference passed to setTodos is identical to the previous one, so React sees 'no change' and may bail out of re-rendering
Arrays are never valid as React state
setTodos ignores any argument that isn't a plain function
explanation: React's state comparison is reference-based (Object.is), not a deep content comparison. Mutating in place keeps the same array reference, so even though the underlying data changed, React can't detect that anything is different and may skip the re-render.

promptText: When a parent component re-renders because its own state changed, what happens to its children by default, even if their props never changed?
options: Children automatically skip re-rendering unless React.memo is explicitly removed
All child components re-render too — React does not automatically bail out based on unchanged props; you must opt in to skipping with React.memo if a subtree's re-render cost is actually a problem
Only child components that use hooks re-render; plain function components without hooks are always skipped
Children re-render only if they are wrapped in a Fragment
explanation: React re-runs the entire subtree by default whenever a parent re-renders, regardless of whether any given child's props actually changed — reconciliation just diffs efficiently afterward. React.memo is the explicit opt-in mechanism to skip a child's re-render when its props are shallowly equal.

promptText: In React 18 development mode, StrictMode mounts a component, runs its effects, unmounts it, and mounts it again. What is this designed to reveal, and what is the WRONG response to it?
options: It reveals effects that leak or duplicate resources due to missing/incorrect cleanup; the wrong response is to suppress the double-invoke (e.g. with a guard ref) instead of fixing the cleanup function
It reveals slow components; the correct response is to wrap them all in React.memo
It is purely cosmetic and has no diagnostic purpose
It reveals bugs only in class components, never in function components using hooks
explanation: The double mount/unmount/remount cycle is a deliberate stress test: if an effect's cleanup correctly reverses its setup, connect → disconnect → connect leaves exactly one live resource, which is harmless. If it instead produces two live connections or duplicate requests, the cleanup is missing or wrong — the fix is always proper cleanup, never suppressing the double-invoke.

promptText: A modal is rendered via `createPortal` into `document.body`, but its JSX is authored inside a component that itself is a child of `<App>`. If the modal button is clicked, does an `onClick` handler on `<App>`'s wrapping div fire?
options: No — since the modal's DOM node lives outside App's DOM subtree, click events never reach App's handler

Yes — React dispatches events according to the React component tree, not the DOM tree, so the click still bubbles up through the modal's logical React ancestors even though its DOM node lives elsewhere
Only if the modal explicitly calls `window.dispatchEvent()`
Only in React versions before 18; this behavior was removed in React 18
explanation: React's synthetic event system bubbles according to the fiber (component) tree, not the physical DOM tree, so a portaled child's events still propagate to its logical React ancestors — even though, at the raw DOM level, the click never passed through those ancestors' actual DOM nodes.

promptText: A React error boundary wraps a component. Which of these errors will it actually catch?
options: An error thrown inside that component's render method
An error thrown inside an onClick handler on a button inside that component
An error from a rejected promise inside a useEffect's async call
Both B and C
explanation: Error boundaries only catch errors thrown during rendering, in lifecycle methods, and in constructors of their child tree — they explicitly do not catch errors in event handlers or in asynchronous code like promise rejections or setTimeout callbacks, which need their own try/catch.

promptText: Two renders both produce a `<UserForm>` element at the same tree position, but the `key` prop changes from `key="user-1"` to `key="user-2"` even though the component type stays identical. What does React do, and why?
options: React reuses the same instance and just re-renders it with new props, since the type is unchanged

React treats (type, key) together as the element's identity; since the key changed, React unmounts the old UserForm instance and mounts a fresh one — discarding all its internal state — even though the type never changed
React throws an error because keys must never change between renders for the same component type
React ignores the key change entirely if the type is identical
explanation: React's reconciler uses (type, key) together as an element's identity at a given position. A changed key — even with the same component type — is treated as 'this is a logically different item,' causing a full unmount and remount with a fresh internal state, which is exactly how the key-reset trick (e.g. keying a form by userId) works.

promptText: A component wrapped in `React.memo` also calls `useContext(SomeContext)`. When that context's Provider value changes, does memoizing the component prevent it from re-rendering?
options: Yes — React.memo blocks any re-render trigger, including context changes

No — React.memo only skips a re-render caused by the parent re-rendering with unchanged props; a context value change is a completely separate re-render trigger that bypasses memo's shallow prop comparison entirely
It depends on whether the context was created with createContext or useContext
Only class components are affected by this; function components wrapped in memo are always protected
explanation: React.memo's shallow prop comparison has nothing to do with context subscriptions — any component (memoized or not) that reads a context via useContext re-renders whenever that context's Provider value reference changes, completely independent of whether its props changed.

promptText: A tooltip measures its own height in an effect to decide whether to flip above or below its trigger. Using `useEffect` for this produces a visible one-frame flicker of the wrong position; switching to `useLayoutEffect` fixes it. Why?
options: useLayoutEffect runs on a separate rendering thread, avoiding any conflict with the browser's paint

useEffect runs asynchronously after the browser has already painted the initial (wrong) position, so the correction is visible for one frame; useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after the DOM mutation but before the browser paints, so the corrected position is what the user sees from the very first frame
useLayoutEffect measures elements more accurately than useEffect due to a different measurement algorithm
There is no real difference; the flicker is caused by an unrelated CSS transition
explanation: useEffect is deliberately deferred until after paint, so any layout correction it makes is visible as a flash of the pre-correction state; useLayoutEffect blocks the browser from painting until it finishes, letting a measure-then-adjust pattern complete invisibly before the frame is ever shown to the user.
